paragraphs: Learning which decisions work is difficult when feedback arrives only as a total loss after an entire episode. The learner cannot directly see which individual actions caused that loss. This paper studies that setting in finite-horizon, tabular Markov decision processes, aiming for algorithms that perform well both when losses follow a stochastic pattern and when they are adversarial.

The proposed algorithms combine a decision-making framework based on occupancy measures with new estimators that extract useful learning signals from episode totals. Occupancy measures describe how frequently a policy visits different state-action combinations. Additional self-bounding arguments support sharper guarantees in stochastic environments, while confidence-based techniques extend the approach to unknown transitions.

With known transitions, the algorithms achieve regret growing as O(log T) in stochastic settings and O(√T) in adversarial settings. Matching lower bounds establish optimality in that setting. The unknown-transition extension is a separate contribution; the abstract does not assign it these same rates. Related results also provide individual-gap-dependent lower bounds and near-optimal algorithms for shortest-path learning with bandit feedback.
neurips-2025-adapting-to-stochastic-and-.tldr: New algorithms learn from episode-total losses while achieving optimal stochastic and adversarial regret rates when transitions are known.

paragraphs: Mathematical problem solving often requires calculations that must be exact and checkable. This paper investigates whether language models can learn to use Python execution through reinforcement learning driven by final outcomes, without supervised examples demonstrating tool use. Its approach, ZeroTIR, trains base models to generate and execute code as part of solving mathematics problems.

The central finding concerns how behavior changes during training. Across the reported experiments, additional training steps correlate strongly with more frequent spontaneous code execution, longer average responses, and higher final accuracy. These observations suggest a measurable relationship between training effort and the development of useful tool-assisted reasoning. They describe observed scaling behavior rather than establishing that every additional step or code execution necessarily improves an answer.

The implementation separates code execution from the training framework and tests the findings across standard reinforcement-learning algorithms and frameworks. ZeroTIR substantially outperforms non-tool ZeroRL baselines on challenging mathematics benchmarks. Together, the results show that outcome rewards can support the acquisition of tool use and provide a reproducible framework for studying how that ability develops.
neurips-2025-agentic-rl-scaling-law-spon.tldr: ZeroTIR learns Python use from outcome rewards, with training progress correlated with more tool execution, longer responses, and better mathematics accuracy.

paragraphs: Multi-task reinforcement learning seeks to solve new tasks using behaviors learned previously, ideally without further interaction. Generalized Policy Improvement combines existing policies and guarantees performance at least as good as the individual policies, but that does not ensure an optimal solution. The Option Keyboard uses a learned meta-policy to combine behaviors dynamically, making the choice of its underlying policies especially important.

This paper provides a method for constructing an optimal behavior basis: a collection of base policies that enables the Option Keyboard to identify optimal solutions without additional interaction for any linear task in the considered framework. The method substantially reduces the number of policies needed to ensure optimality. This addresses the computational burden associated with constructing a Convex Coverage Set, another route to optimality for linear rewards.

The authors also prove that the resulting construction is strictly more expressive than a Convex Coverage Set, supporting optimal solutions for particular classes of nonlinear tasks. That extension does not cover every nonlinear task. Experiments in challenging domains show improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, with larger advantages as task complexity increases.
neurips-2025-constructing-an-optimal-beh.tldr: An efficiently constructed behavior basis lets the Option Keyboard solve new linear tasks optimally and extends optimality to certain nonlinear tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains language models to better match human preferences. Its success can depend on assumptions about how people compare responses, which reference policy anchors training, and how rewards are represented. When those assumptions are wrong, fine-tuning can move the model in undesirable directions. This paper addresses that sensitivity through a new preference-optimization algorithm.

The method is doubly robust: it remains consistent if either the preference model or the reference policy is correctly specified. Both do not have to be correct simultaneously. This matters because an alignment procedure can otherwise depend on getting several modeling choices right together. The guarantee offers two alternative routes to consistency, while still requiring correctness of at least one of those two components.

The authors report stronger and more robust performance than state-of-the-art algorithms in both theoretical analysis and practical evaluation. The contribution is therefore an alignment method with a specific statistical protection against misspecification, supported by empirical results. Its stated guarantee should be understood through the preference-model-or-reference-policy condition, rather than as protection against arbitrary errors in every part of an alignment pipeline.
neurips-2025-doubly-robust-alignment-for.tldr: Doubly robust preference optimization remains consistent when either its preference model or its reference policy is correctly specified.

paragraphs: Explainable clustering assigns data points to groups through a decision tree whose internal nodes compare one feature against a threshold. Each assignment can therefore be traced through simple decisions. This paper studies how to construct such trees while keeping the k-medians clustering cost close to its optimum, including when data points are continually inserted or deleted.

The algorithm supports every finite ℓp norm with p at least one, extending previous results that covered only p = 1 and p = 2. Its approximation guarantee is Õ(p(log k)^(1 + 1/p − 1/p²)), where k is the number of clusters. For p = 2, this improves the previous bound. For p = 1, it matches the tight known bound up to an O(log log k) multiplicative factor.

The dynamic implementation maintains an explainable clustering with amortized update time O(d log³ k), where d is the number of features, and O(log k) recourse. These guarantees connect interpretability with efficient maintenance: the method controls both clustering quality and the work and changes associated with updating an evolving dataset.
neurips-2025-dynamic-algorithm-for-expla.tldr: A new algorithm provides explainable k-medians clustering across all finite ℓp norms and supports efficient updates as data changes.

paragraphs: Recognizing that a video contains a physical activity is different from understanding the skill involved in performing it. ExAct evaluates this more demanding capability through questions about expert-level physical human activities. The benchmark contains 3,521 expert-curated video question-answer pairs covering 11 activities across sports, bike repair, cooking, health, music, and dance.

Each question requires selecting one answer from five carefully designed options. The evaluation is intended to require fine-grained understanding of skilled actions, making the distinctions between candidate answers central to the task. This creates a focused way to examine whether a vision-language model can interpret the details of physical and procedural skills.

The evaluated models show a substantial gap relative to trained human experts. The best-performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, achieves 55.35% accuracy, compared with 82.02% for the experts. These results identify expert action understanding as a remaining challenge within the tested setting. By releasing the dataset and code, the authors provide a resource for developing and comparing models aimed at more precise interpretation of skilled human behavior.
neurips-2025-exact-a-video-language-benc.tldr: ExAct tests expert understanding of skilled actions in video and reveals a substantial accuracy gap between leading models and human experts.

paragraphs: Fair resource allocation can depend on what resources accomplish for different groups, not simply on how much each group receives. This paper formalizes that perspective through Equality of Impact, a fairness criterion built from group-level impact functions. It generalizes equality of opportunity and guides the allocation of resources that can be divided continuously.

The study focuses on two groups whose allocation outcomes are initially unknown and exhibit diminishing marginal effects: additional resources have progressively smaller effects. Within this setting, the authors develop methods that seek high total welfare while minimizing violations of Equality of Impact. Their formulation accommodates a broader class of welfare dynamics than the prior work they discuss.

For environments without noise, an online algorithm exploits the problem's geometry and achieves constant cumulative fairness regret. This controls accumulated fairness regret over time, rather than asserting that every individual allocation has zero violation. A meta-algorithm extends the approach to noisy environments. Empirical evaluations show that the methods find fair allocations and perform competitively against representative baselines, connecting the fairness criterion to an implementable learning procedure.
neurips-2025-fair-continuous-resource-al.tldr: Equality of Impact guides online resource allocation toward fair outcomes and high welfare when group responses are unknown and have diminishing marginal effects.

paragraphs: Quantizing a vision transformer reduces the numerical precision used to represent its computations, making low-bit models attractive for reducing computational demands. Existing approaches face a tradeoff: post-training quantization can lose substantial accuracy, while quantization-aware training can be expensive and unstable. GPLQ proposes a two-stage process designed to retain accuracy and downstream generalization with much less training.

The design follows two empirical observations: activation quantization is especially important, and preserving the model's original optimization basin matters for generalization. First, GPLQ quantizes activations while keeping weights in full precision. It uses a feature-mimicking loss for one epoch to help preserve the model's existing behavior. Second, it quantizes the weights using a post-training method.

The authors report that GPLQ is 100 times faster than existing quantization-aware training methods and uses less memory than full-precision training. Its 4-bit models remain highly competitive with full-precision models on ImageNet accuracy and on downstream tasks, including fine-grained classification and object detection. These findings support separating activation adaptation from weight quantization as an effective efficiency strategy.
neurips-2025-gplq-a-general-practical-an.tldr: GPLQ quantizes activations before weights, producing competitive 4-bit vision transformers with substantially lower training time and memory use.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that explain relationships in data. Its search can waste effort on different representations of equivalent expressions. It also struggles when useful feedback, such as whether an expression obeys a physical law, becomes available only after the expression is complete. This paper addresses both problems within a single framework.

Graph-based Symbolic Regression represents candidate formulas as Expression Graphs. A term-rewriting system and directed acyclic graph structure encode expression equivalences and provide a permutation-invariant representation, compressing the search space. The search itself uses hybrid neural-guided Monte Carlo tree search. Neural guidance incorporates information about whole-expression constraints, while an adaptive exploration policy balances investigating alternatives against pursuing promising candidates.

The theoretical results establish uniqueness of the proposed graph representation and convergence of the search algorithm. Experiments on synthetic data and real scientific datasets demonstrate efficient, accurate expression discovery and adherence to physical laws. The combined contribution is a way to avoid redundant formula exploration while bringing scientific constraints into the search process, rather than relying solely on feedback from finished candidates.
neurips-2025-graph-based-symbolic-regres.tldr: GSR combines equivalence-aware expression graphs with constraint-guided search to discover accurate mathematical formulas more efficiently.

paragraphs: Large graphs present language models with more information than their context windows can comfortably hold, while different analysis tasks require different sequences of operations. GraphChain addresses these challenges by having a language model coordinate specialized tools dynamically. The resulting analysis proceeds through a sequence of tool-assisted steps resembling an exploratory workflow.

Its first component, Progressive Graph Distillation, uses reinforcement learning to generate tool sequences that balance relevance to the task with compression of intermediate states. This makes the amount of information carried forward part of the learned strategy. Its second component, Structure-aware Test-Time Adaptation, uses a lightweight self-supervised adapter conditioned on graph spectral properties. The adapter supplies soft prompts to a frozen language-model policy, allowing adaptation to different graph structures without retraining that policy.

Experiments show significant improvements over prior methods. The approach connects two requirements for scalable graph analysis: keeping intermediate information manageable and adjusting behavior to structural differences between graphs. Its stated results support tool chaining and lightweight adaptation as complementary ways to improve language-model-driven graph analysis.
neurips-2025-graphchain-large-language-m.tldr: GraphChain learns tool sequences that compress graph information and adapts a frozen language-model policy to different graph structures.

paragraphs: A model can describe an image convincingly while still leaving uncertainty about its understanding of the scene's underlying structure. IR3D-Bench tests that understanding through reconstruction. Given an image, a vision-language agent must use programming and rendering tools to recreate the scene's three-dimensional structure, turning visual interpretation into an active creation task.

The benchmark follows analysis by synthesis: understanding is assessed through what the agent can build from its observations. This expands evaluation beyond descriptions or conversational answers to include the agent's ability to coordinate tools and produce a reconstruction. Its metrics examine geometric accuracy, spatial relationships, appearance attributes, and overall plausibility, making several aspects of reconstruction quality explicit.

Initial experiments with state-of-the-art vision-language models reveal limitations concentrated particularly in visual precision rather than basic tool operation. Successful tool use therefore does not, by itself, imply an accurate recreation of the observed scene. The released data and evaluation protocols provide a framework for studying that distinction and improving agents whose scene understanding must support concrete visual creation.
neurips-2025-ir3d-bench-evaluating-visio.tldr: IR3D-Bench tests scene understanding through tool-driven 3D reconstruction, revealing visual precision as a key weakness in evaluated models.

paragraphs: Formal Bayesian modeling can require expertise and time that domain specialists do not have. Large Language Bayes starts instead from observed data and an informal description of the problem. It combines a language model with a probabilistic programming language to represent uncertainty jointly over formal models, latent variables, and data.

The method does not simply choose one generated model and treat it as settled. It obtains a posterior over latent variables by conditioning on observations and averaging over possible formal models. To approximate this difficult inference problem, the proposed recipe generates many models, performs approximate inference within each, and combines their results through a weighted average.

The authors justify and analyze this procedure using self-normalized importance sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and importance-weighted variational inference. Experiments produce sensible predictions using only the data and informal description, without requiring the user to specify a formal model. The contribution is a route from informal domain knowledge to Bayesian predictions that incorporates uncertainty across candidate model formulations into the inference process.
neurips-2025-large-language-bayes-50f702.tldr: Large Language Bayes generates and averages over formal models to make Bayesian predictions from data and an informal problem description.

paragraphs: Removing layers makes a language model smaller, but can also discard useful capabilities. This paper identifies weaknesses in direct layer removal, linear weighted layer aggregation, and existing recovery procedures. Its method, CoMe, reduces model size progressively while attempting to preserve important information from the layers being compressed.

CoMe first scores channels using both activation intensity and weight norms. These measurements guide a fine-grained selection of important channels. It then concatenates selected channels from adjacent layers to merge their useful content as compression proceeds. After pruning, hierarchical distillation transfers knowledge from the original model to the smaller one, using layer correspondences established during the pruning process.

Across seven benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. In the stated LLaMA-2-7b result, removing 30% of the parameters preserves 83% of the original model's average accuracy. That figure expresses retained accuracy relative to the original model, rather than an absolute accuracy score. The findings support compression that combines selective merging with targeted recovery, allowing the smaller model to retain some capabilities that straightforward layer deletion would lose.
neurips-2025-layer-as-puzzle-pieces-comp.tldr: CoMe compresses language models by merging important channels across adjacent layers and then transferring knowledge through hierarchical distillation.

paragraphs: Long videos contain too many frames to inspect densely while also keeping their full context inside a limited model input. MR. Video organizes the problem around MapReduce: analyze short segments independently, then combine their results into a response informed by the whole video. This makes local detail and global context separate but connected parts of the computation.

The Map operations perform dense perception on short segments in parallel. Reduce operations aggregate those analyses into a globally informed answer. The video-agent implementation also keeps character and object names consistent across captions, helping connect actions over long periods. A question-intention analysis step locates relevant information by reasoning jointly about the question and the video's broader context.

The authors report an accuracy improvement of more than 7% on LVBench over state-of-the-art video agents and vision-language models, alongside advantages on multiple long-video benchmarks. These findings support MapReduce as a useful system-level organization for video understanding. The additional naming and question-analysis mechanisms help ensure that dividing a video into segments does not prevent reasoning across its full duration.
neurips-2025-mr-video-mapreduce-as-an-ef.tldr: MR. Video combines parallel segment analysis with global aggregation and consistent naming to improve long-video understanding.

paragraphs: This paper studies a mixture-of-experts view of fine-tuning in which a pretrained model remains fixed while a new trainable expert, or prompt, is added. A softmax gating mechanism determines how the experts contribute. The statistical question is how accurately the gating and prompt parameters can be estimated as more observations become available.

The authors analyze maximum likelihood estimation and introduce a formal notion of distinguishability between the pretrained model and the new prompt. The key difficulty arises when the prompt acquires knowledge that overlaps with the fixed model. As their contributions become harder to distinguish, identifying the parameters that govern those contributions also becomes more difficult.

When the distinguishability condition holds, the paper derives minimax-optimal estimation rates for all gating and prompt parameters. When it fails, the rates become significantly slower and depend on how quickly the prompt approaches the pretrained model. Numerical experiments corroborate these theoretical findings. The result connects a specific statistical obstacle in prompt-based fine-tuning to overlap between the original and added experts, rather than treating parameter estimation as equally straightforward across all such models.
neurips-2025-on-minimax-estimation-of-pa.tldr: Parameter estimation in softmax-contaminated mixtures of experts slows substantially when the trainable prompt becomes difficult to distinguish from the pretrained model.

paragraphs: Graph attention allows a node to gather information from other nodes, but gathering many messages can make the important ones harder to preserve. This paper identifies an effect called over-aggregating: a large volume of messages is combined with insufficient discrimination, diluting useful information and potentially losing details that matter for the task.

Wideformer addresses the problem through a plug-and-play modification to graph attention. It divides aggregation into parallel processes so that each aggregation handles a smaller volume of input. A guidance step then sorts and weights the outputs, encouraging the model to concentrate on informative subsets. Splitting the work and prioritizing its results address different parts of the same dilution problem.

Evaluations show that Wideformer mitigates over-aggregating and improves the performance of the backbone methods relative to baselines. The stated findings support a distinction between accessing global information and effectively selecting from it: broad access alone can still leave useful messages obscured. Wideformer's contribution is an aggregation design that helps existing attention methods retain and emphasize those messages.
neurips-2025-relieving-the-over-aggregat.tldr: Wideformer splits graph attention aggregation into parallel processes and prioritizes their outputs to reduce dilution of important messages.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, communication patterns influence how efficiently participating nodes approach global averaging. Dynamic graphs change those communication connections over time. This paper revisits the one-peer exponential graph, whose known finite-time convergence property applies when the number of nodes is a power of two, and studies its efficiency for arbitrary node counts.

The analysis examines principles behind the graph's behavior, including the expected spectral gap and whether mixing matrices commute. These matrices describe the averaging operations associated with communication, and commutativity concerns whether their order changes their combined effect. The authors use the resulting understanding to construct two alternatives: the k-peer exponential graph and the null-cascade graph.

The null-cascade graph achieves finite-time convergence for any number of nodes while preserving commutativity. This removes the power-of-two restriction attached to the stated finite-time property of the one-peer design. Experiments confirm the effectiveness of the new graphs, especially null-cascade, in most tested settings. The empirical qualification matters: the reported advantage spans most settings examined, rather than establishing superiority for every decentralized-learning configuration.
neurips-2025-revisiting-1-peer-exponenti.tldr: New communication graphs improve decentralized learning, with null-cascade achieving finite-time averaging convergence for any node count and commuting mixing matrices.

paragraphs: Referring image segmentation identifies the pixels belonging to an object described in natural language. Simple expressions can often be handled through keyword matching, but more ambiguous descriptions require contextual reasoning. This paper highlights two difficult cases: descriptions mentioning multiple entities that can distract from the target, and descriptions that never explicitly name the target's object category.

SaFiRe approaches these cases through repeated cycles of broad understanding followed by detailed inspection. The design is inspired by a two-phase human cognitive process. It uses Mamba's scan-then-update behavior to support the phased computation and enable multiple rounds of refinement with linear complexity. This gives the framework a mechanism for revisiting and refining an initial interpretation.

The authors also introduce aRefCOCO, a benchmark designed around ambiguous referring expressions. Experiments on both standard datasets and the new benchmark show that SaFiRe outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution combines an architectural response to ambiguity with a way to evaluate it, extending the task beyond identifying objects from short, explicit noun phrases toward interpreting descriptions whose target depends on context.
neurips-2025-safire-saccade-fixation-rei.tldr: SaFiRe uses repeated global and detailed inspection to segment objects from ambiguous descriptions, evaluated partly through the new aRefCOCO benchmark.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means recognizing unfamiliar combinations of concepts that a model already knows. Evaluating this ability is difficult because existing protocols lack standardization and can trade rigor for computational efficiency. This paper addresses both evaluation and model design, focusing on supervised vision systems and the architectural biases that help them generalize compositionally.

The proposed evaluation framework unifies and extends earlier approaches while reducing its computational requirements from combinatorial to constant. The authors use it in an extensive study involving more than 5,000 trained models. This supplies a broad empirical assessment of compositional generalization in modern supervised vision backbones alongside the new evaluation procedure.

The paper also introduces Attribute Invariant Networks, designed to improve the tradeoff between compositional performance and model overhead. The authors report a 23.43% accuracy improvement over baselines and a reduction in parameter overhead from 600% to 16% relative to fully disentangled counterparts. Their claimed new Pareto frontier concerns this joint tradeoff: the models achieve stronger compositional generalization without requiring the parameter expansion associated with those counterparts.
neurips-2025-scalable-evaluation-and-neu.tldr: A scalable evaluation framework and Attribute Invariant Networks improve the measurement and efficiency of compositional generalization in vision models.

paragraphs: Sequence schemas are reusable structures that help a learner adapt to new tasks sharing a familiar order or organization. This paper studies how such structures develop through shaping, a curriculum that progresses from simple subtasks to complete sequences. The authors train recurrent neural networks on an odor-sequence task using a protocol inspired by experimental neuroscience.

The trained networks reproduce key features of schema learning observed in the orbitofrontal cortex: rapid adaptation, structured geometry in neural representations, and progressively compressed dimensionality. Analysis links the learned schemas to sequence attractors. During shaping, initially separate attractors develop into connected sequences and eventually into more generalizable dynamics capturing structure shared across task variations.

A keyword-spotting application also shows that shaping supports rapid development of sequence-attractor-like schemas and improves learning efficiency. Together, these results provide a proposed dynamical mechanism for how a curriculum can produce reusable sequential knowledge. The biological connection rests on reproducing reported features of schema learning in the model, while the attractor analysis explains how that behavior arises within the trained networks.
neurips-2025-shaping-sequence-attractor-.tldr: Shaping recurrent networks from simple tasks to full sequences produces attractor dynamics that support reusable schemas and faster adaptation.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a vision-language model improve its predictions using the data it encounters after training. A challenge is retaining useful information as more test samples arrive. Statistics Caching Adaptation, or SCA, addresses this by accumulating task-specific information from all encountered samples through compact statistics, instead of keeping a collection of raw feature vectors.

The method formulates the reuse of previous features as a least-squares problem. That formulation allows the relevant feature statistics to be updated incrementally, supporting online adaptation without a fixed-size feature cache. The accumulated information can therefore continue to incorporate earlier observations as new ones arrive, rather than depending on which individual features remain stored.

SCA also uses prediction uncertainty to reduce the influence of noisy pseudo-labels and to adjust the balance between multiple prediction sources. These mechanisms address reliability alongside memory management: retaining past information is more useful when uncertain predictions receive appropriate treatment. Experiments report strong performance with competitive computational efficiency, supporting statistical accumulation as a practical way to sustain adaptation over a stream of test samples.
neurips-2025-statistics-caching-test-tim.tldr: SCA adapts vision-language models online by retaining compact feature statistics and using uncertainty to manage noisy predictions.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected by a different behavior policy. Long decision sequences and high-dimensional states make this difficult: importance weighting can suffer large variance, while learned dynamics can accumulate prediction errors. STITCH-OPE uses generative trajectory modeling to address these challenges without requiring direct evaluation through new environmental interaction.

The framework begins with a diffusion model pretrained on behavior-policy data. During denoising, guidance based on the target policy's score steers generated trajectories toward that policy. It subtracts the behavior policy's score to prevent over-regularization, and constructs long trajectories by joining shorter generated sections end to end.

Under assumptions described as mild, the authors prove that these modifications produce an exponential variance reduction relative to long-horizon trajectory diffusion. This theoretical comparison is specific to that reference approach. Experiments on D4RL and OpenAI Gym additionally show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art off-policy evaluation methods in mean squared error, correlation, and regret. The results support combining corrected guidance with trajectory stitching for evaluating policies over long horizons.
neurips-2025-stitch-ope-trajectory-stitc.tldr: STITCH-OPE combines policy-guided diffusion with stitched trajectory segments to improve long-horizon off-policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds seek to explain how training performance relates to performance on new data. Information-theoretic bounds connect that question to the information a learning algorithm retains about its training sample. This paper develops new conditional mutual information bounds using stochastic projection and lossy compression, obtaining guarantees that are generally tighter than existing ones.

A key result concerns particular problem instances where earlier mutual-information or conditional-mutual-information bounds become uninformative or fail to capture the correct behavior. For those instances, the new bounds provide generalization guarantees of order O(1/√n), where n is the training-set size. This is a result for the identified instances, rather than an unrestricted rate claim for every learning problem.

The authors also examine claims that good prediction can require memorizing a large fraction of training data. They show that every learning algorithm has an auxiliary algorithm that does not memorize and achieves comparable generalization error for any data distribution. This existence result supports their conclusion that memorization is not necessary for good generalization, while distinguishing predictive behavior from how much training information an algorithm retains.
neurips-2025-tighter-cmi-based-generaliz.tldr: Projection and compression yield tighter information-based generalization bounds and support the existence of non-memorizing algorithms with comparable generalization.

paragraphs: An assistant intended to help prevent harm must recognize potential dangers even when a user has not explicitly asked about them. Proactive Safety Bench, or PaSBench, evaluates that ability through scenarios involving people's behavior and surroundings. It contains 416 scenarios across five safety-critical domains, comprising 128 image sequences and 288 text logs.

The authors evaluate 36 advanced models and find substantial weaknesses in proactive risk recognition. A leading performer, Gemini-2.5-pro, reaches 71% accuracy on images and 64% on text, yet the reported repeated-trial evaluation finds missed risks in the 45–55% range. The repeated testing highlights reliability concerns that are not fully conveyed by a single aggregate accuracy result.

Failure analysis identifies unstable proactive reasoning, rather than missing knowledge, as the primary limitation in the evaluated models. This shifts attention toward whether a model consistently applies relevant knowledge to notice danger without prompting. The benchmark and findings provide a basis for studying more dependable protective assistants, while documenting that the tested systems still struggle with the proactive behavior such an application would require.
neurips-2025-towards-evaluating-proactiv.tldr: PaSBench finds that advanced models often miss everyday risks, with failure analysis pointing primarily to unstable proactive reasoning.

paragraphs: Generating an image with several specific subjects requires control over both who appears and how each subject is depicted. Pose, style, and lighting must remain editable without interfering with identity or overall coherence. This paper addresses the artifacts and entangled attributes that can arise when adding such control to Diffusion Transformers.

XVerse converts reference images into offsets applied to token-specific modulation in the model's text stream. This gives the generation process subject-specific controls without disrupting image latents or features. The placement of the control matters: reference information influences the text-side modulation associated with particular subjects, supporting precise and independent adjustments within a scene containing multiple subjects.

The authors report high-fidelity multi-subject synthesis that remains editable, with robust control over individual characteristics and semantic attributes. The stated contribution is a mechanism for combining reference-based identity preservation with fine-grained scene editing in one generation model. Its significance lies in making personalized, complex scenes easier to control while preserving the coherence that can be undermined when subject attributes interfere with one another.
neurips-2025-xverse-consistent-multi-sub.tldr: XVerse uses reference-driven text-stream modulation to independently control subject identities and semantic attributes in multi-subject image generation.
